claims.title: Authorization codes can be sent to a prefix-matched redirect destination
claims.description: An outside attacker operating a registered partner integration can request authorization with an attacker-controlled redirect URI that merely starts with a registered URI. `process:authorization-server` accepts that prefix match and `flow:entity:member>entity:partner-app>return-with-authorization-code` returns the member's authorization code to the selected redirect destination. The attacker can recover the code and exchange it as the partner client; the resulting bearer access token can then be presented on `flow:entity:partner-app>process:rewards-api>call-rewards-api` to read the member's balance and transaction-related data. This depends on the attacker being able to supply a controlled URI satisfying the prefix comparison; it is not a claim that every registered redirect URI is attacker-controlled.

quotes.text: the authorization server accepts any redirect URI that starts with it
The browser then returns to the partner app's redirect URI with an authorization code.

severity.justification: Likelihood is medium because `flow:entity:member>entity:partner-app>return-with-authorization-code` crosses from member devices to partner servers and the authorization server uses a stated prefix redirect match, although exploitation requires a controlled matching URI and member authorization. Impact is high because the returned authorization code is a credential that can be exchanged for a bearer token usable on the partner-to-`process:rewards-api` flow, which carries `financial`, `pii`, and `credentials` assets.

mitigations.detail: Make `process:authorization-server` compare normalized redirect URIs as exact values, rather than accepting a URI by prefix, and reject unregistered query, path, host, scheme, or port variants.

mitigations.summary: Bind authorization codes to the requesting client and PKCE verifier
mitigations.detail: Require PKCE for public clients and bind each authorization code to its client ID, exact redirect URI, and verifier so a recovered code cannot be exchanged by another recipient.

claims.title: Identity-database credentials may be readable on the unverified authorization-server connection
claims.description: `flow:process:authorization-server>store:identity-database>read-and-write-accounts-and-grants` carries password hashes, authorization codes, refresh tokens, consents, and member account data between `process:authorization-server` and `store:identity-database`, but its `encryption_in_transit` value is unknown. If that internal segment is not protected, an attacker able to observe the cloud path can intercept those credentials and PII. Recovered refresh tokens or codes can be exchanged at `process:authorization-server`, and the resulting access tokens reach `process:rewards-api` and its member financial and PII operations. This draft is conditional on the unverified transport attribute, not an assertion that the connection is plaintext.

quotes.text: The authorization server keeps member accounts, email addresses and password hashes in the identity database, together with the authorization codes, refresh tokens and consents it issues.

severity.justification: Likelihood is low and conditional because the connection's `encryption_in_transit` is unknown and the attacker must obtain an observation position on an internal rewards-cloud segment. Impact is high because the flow carries password hashes and reusable authorization credentials as well as member PII, and recovered tokens can reach the internet-facing rewards API.

mitigations.summary: Verify and enforce encrypted database transport
mitigations.detail: Establish the transport posture for `flow:process:authorization-server>store:identity-database>read-and-write-accounts-and-grants`, require TLS 1.2+ with certificate validation, and prefer mTLS for the authorization-server/database connection.

mitigations.summary: Reduce the value of intercepted authorization artifacts
mitigations.detail: Use short-lived, single-use authorization codes; rotate refresh tokens on use; and bind token exchanges to their client and PKCE verifier.

claims.title: Points-ledger balances may be readable on an unverified API-to-ledger connection
claims.description: `flow:process:rewards-api>store:points-ledger>read-and-write-points` transfers balances and points transactions from `process:rewards-api` to `store:points-ledger`, while `encryption_in_transit` is unknown. If transport protection is absent on that segment, an attacker with an on-path position can intercept members' financial activity and balance information. The collected records allow targeted use of data exposed by `process:rewards-api` and reveal every affected member's rewards activity; this is conditional on the unknown transport setting.

quotes.text: The rewards API reads and writes the points ledger, which holds every member's balance and every points transaction.
Nobody recorded how the rewards API connects to the ledger

severity.justification: Likelihood is low and conditional because `encryption_in_transit` for the API-to-ledger flow is unknown and exploitation requires access to that internal path. Impact is high because `store:points-ledger` holds every member's balances and transactions and is tagged `financial` and `business-critical-data`.

mitigations.summary: Encrypt and authenticate the API-to-ledger hop
mitigations.detail: Require TLS 1.2+ with validated server identity, preferably mTLS, for `flow:process:rewards-api>store:points-ledger>read-and-write-points` and record the setting in the system model.

mitigations.summary: Minimize transaction data on the connection
mitigations.detail: Use opaque member and transaction references where the ledger can resolve them, reducing exposed financial detail if a transport endpoint is compromised.

claims.title: Bearer tokens may be readable while the API writes request logs
claims.description: `flow:process:rewards-api>store:api-log-store>write-request-log` carries every request header, including bearer access tokens, but its `encryption_in_transit` value is unknown. If the internal logging transport is unencrypted, an on-path attacker can intercept reusable bearer tokens and the PII or financial request context sent beside them. The attacker can then use a recovered token against `process:rewards-api` through the mobile-app or partner-app API flows, obtaining the data and operations permitted by that token. This is conditional on the unverified transport setting.

quotes.text: The rewards API also writes every request it receives, headers included, to the API log store.

severity.justification: Likelihood is low and conditional because the logging flow's `encryption_in_transit` is unknown and an attacker must observe an internal connection. Impact is high because the flow explicitly includes bearer access tokens, which are reusable credentials, alongside API requests involving financial and PII assets.

mitigations.detail: Require TLS with authenticated endpoints for `flow:process:rewards-api>store:api-log-store>write-request-log`, including any internal log-shipping hop.
Remove or tokenize Authorization headers at `process:rewards-api` before log emission so the log flow and `store:api-log-store` never contain replayable bearer tokens.

claims.title: Account-closure records may be exposed on an unverified support-console connection
claims.description: `flow:process:support-console>store:identity-database>close-accounts` has unknown `encryption_in_transit` while `process:support-console` submits account-closure updates to `store:identity-database`. If this connection lacks transport protection, an attacker able to observe the internal path can intercept closure events and associated account identifiers, disclosing member account status and PII. The observations also identify accounts whose retained refresh tokens remain in the identity database, aiding later targeting; this draft is conditional on the unknown transport control.

quotes.text: Nobody recorded how the support console connects to the identity database
Closing an account marks it closed in the identity database. Nothing happens to that member's refresh tokens, which sit in the same database.

severity.justification: Likelihood is low and conditional because the support-console connection's `encryption_in_transit` is unknown and the attacker needs an internal observation position. Impact is medium because the flow reveals account-closure activity and identifiers associated with `store:identity-database`, which is tagged `pii` and `credentials`.

mitigations.summary: Protect support-console database traffic with mTLS
mitigations.detail: Determine and enforce TLS with authenticated peers for `flow:process:support-console>store:identity-database>close-accounts`, rather than relying on its rewards-cloud placement.
Use opaque account references and avoid transmitting unnecessary member fields on the closure operation.

claims.title: A copied identity database exposes credentials if at-rest encryption is absent
claims.description: `store:identity-database` contains member accounts, email addresses, password hashes, authorization codes, refresh tokens, and consents, but its `encryption_at_rest` attribute is unknown. If this resolves to storage without encryption at rest, an attacker who obtains a copied volume, snapshot, backup, or decommissioned medium can read those records without authenticating through `process:authorization-server`. Recovered refresh tokens and authorization artifacts can be exchanged through the authorization server and then used to reach `process:rewards-api`; this is conditional on the unknown at-rest control rather than an assertion that encryption is absent.

quotes.text: The authorization server keeps member accounts, email addresses and password hashes in the identity database, together with the authorization codes, refresh tokens and consents it issues.
Nobody recorded how any of the three stores is protected at rest.

severity.justification: Likelihood is medium and conditional because `store:identity-database` has unknown `encryption_at_rest`, and obtaining an operational copy does not require live application access if that protection is absent. Impact is high because the store is tagged `credentials` and `pii` and holds password hashes plus reusable refresh-token and authorization artifacts.

mitigations.summary: Encrypt the identity database and all operational copies
mitigations.detail: Establish the current state, then require envelope encryption with KMS-managed keys for `store:identity-database`, backups, snapshots, replicas, and decommissioned media.

mitigations.summary: Restrict storage-copy export and key use
mitigations.detail: Use separate least-privilege backup and restore roles, restrict snapshot export, and audit KMS decrypt operations for identity-database material.

claims.title: A copied points ledger exposes all member reward activity if at-rest encryption is absent
claims.description: `store:points-ledger` holds every member's balance and every points transaction, and its `encryption_at_rest` attribute is unknown. If the store or its operational copies are not encrypted at rest, an attacker holding a backup, snapshot, replica, or removed storage medium can read the ledger directly without using `process:rewards-api`. One copied artifact discloses the rewards activity of the full member population, which can be correlated with the API's member-facing financial operations. This draft is conditional on the unresolved at-rest encryption setting.

quotes.text: The rewards API reads and writes the points ledger, which holds every member's balance and every points transaction.
Nobody recorded how any of the three stores is protected at rest.

severity.justification: Likelihood is medium and conditional because `store:points-ledger` has unknown `encryption_at_rest`, and a copied backup or snapshot bypasses the API access path if encryption is absent. Impact is high because the store contains every member's balances and transactions and is tagged `financial` and `business-critical-data`.

mitigations.summary: Encrypt ledger media and copies with managed keys
mitigations.detail: Require encryption at rest for `store:points-ledger`, backups, snapshots, and replicas, with KMS-held keys and restricted decrypt permissions.
Separate backup/export principals from application principals and log snapshot creation, restoration, export, and data-access operations.

claims.title: A copied API log store exposes bearer credentials if at-rest encryption is absent
claims.description: `store:api-log-store` stores every request received by `process:rewards-api`, including headers that contain bearer access tokens, while its `encryption_at_rest` value is unknown. If this store or an operational copy lacks encryption at rest, an attacker with a snapshot, backup, or removed storage copy can read replayable access tokens and associated request context without authenticating to the rewards API. Those tokens can be used against `process:rewards-api` via its mobile or partner API flows, extending a log-store disclosure into member PII and financial-data access. This is conditional on the unresolved at-rest encryption state.

quotes.text: The rewards API also writes every request it receives, headers included, to the API log store.
Nobody recorded how any of the three stores is protected at rest.

severity.justification: Likelihood is medium and conditional because `store:api-log-store` has unknown `encryption_at_rest` and operational copies can be acquired independently of the live API if storage encryption is absent. Impact is high because the log store is tagged `credentials` and `pii` and explicitly holds bearer access tokens usable at the internet-facing rewards API.

mitigations.summary: Stop recording bearer credentials in API logs
mitigations.detail: Redact Authorization headers and any token-bearing parameters at `process:rewards-api` before data reaches `store:api-log-store`; rotate any tokens already captured.

mitigations.summary: Encrypt and tightly control log-store copies
mitigations.detail: Enforce KMS-backed encryption at rest on `store:api-log-store` and all backups, snapshots, and replicas, with log access and key-use permissions at least as restrictive as the source API data.
